chapter_title: Redis Cluster: Sharding for Horizontal Scaling
chapter_summary:
While Redis replication with Sentinel provides high availability, it doesn't solve the problem of scaling beyond the capacity of a single master instance. A single master is limited by the amount of RAM it can hold and the CPU it can utilize for write operations. To overcome these limitations and achieve true horizontal scaling, Redis introduced **Redis Cluster**. Redis Cluster is a distributed implementation of Redis that automatically shards your data across multiple Redis nodes. This means your dataset is partitioned, with different parts residing on different nodes, allowing you to store much larger datasets and handle a higher throughput of operations than a single Redis instance could. Sharding is the key concept here: instead of one large database, you have several smaller, independent databases that collectively form a single logical database.

The core idea behind Redis Cluster is the concept of **hash slots**. The entire keyspace is divided into 16384 hash slots. Each key in Redis is mapped to one of these slots using a simple hashing algorithm: `CRC16(key) % 16384`. When you add a key to Redis Cluster, the cluster determines which slot it belongs to and directs the operation to the node responsible for that slot. Each node in a Redis Cluster is responsible for a subset of the 16384 hash slots. For example, Node A might handle slots 0-5000, Node B slots 5001-10000, and Node C slots 10001-16383. This distribution allows the dataset to be spread across multiple machines, overcoming the memory and CPU constraints of a single server.

A Redis Cluster is composed of multiple Redis instances, each playing a specific role. Every node in the cluster holds a portion of the hash slots and can act as a master for those slots. To ensure high availability within the cluster, each master node can have one or more replica nodes. These replicas function similarly to standalone replicas, mirroring the data of their respective masters. If a master node fails, its replicas can be promoted to take over its slots, ensuring continuous service. This means Redis Cluster combines both sharding for horizontal scaling and replication for high availability. Clients connecting to a Redis Cluster are "cluster-aware." They don't connect to a single node, but rather use a smart client library that understands the cluster's topology. When a client sends a command for a specific key, the client library calculates the hash slot for that key and directly sends the command to the correct node responsible for that slot. If the client sends a command to the wrong node, that node will respond with a `MOVED` redirection error, telling the client which node is responsible for the slot, and the client will then retry the command on the correct node.

Redis Cluster offers significant benefits for large-scale applications. It allows you to scale your Redis deployment almost linearly by adding more nodes, increasing both storage capacity and throughput. It also provides automatic failover, as replicas can take over from failed masters without manual intervention. However, it also introduces some trade-offs. The most notable limitation is that **multi-key operations are only supported if all keys involved belong to the same hash slot**. For example, `MGET` or `DEL` commands involving keys in different slots will fail. To work around this, Redis Cluster supports "hash tags," where you can force multiple keys into the same slot by enclosing a part of the key in curly braces `{}`. For example, `user:{100}:profile` and `user:{100}:cart` would both map to the same hash slot because the hash is computed only on `{100}`. This allows you to perform multi-key operations on related data.

Another important aspect is that Redis Cluster does not support certain commands or features that rely on a global view of the dataset, such as `KEYS` (which iterates over all keys in the entire cluster) or `SELECT` (which switches databases, as Redis Cluster only supports database 0). For safety, when designing your data model for Redis Cluster, always consider how your keys will be distributed and whether your application requires multi-key operations across different slots. If your application heavily relies on such operations for unrelated keys, Redis Cluster might not be the most suitable solution, and you might need to rethink your data partitioning strategy or consider alternative scaling approaches. Understanding these limitations upfront is crucial for a successful Redis Cluster deployment.

screens.title: Redis Cluster: Sharding for Horizontal Scaling
screens.subtitle: How Redis partitions your keyspace so you can grow past a single node

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn why a single master Redis server reaches practical limits and how Redis Cluster solves that by sharding data across multiple nodes. Sharding splits a large dataset into smaller pieces that live on different machines, allowing both memory and write throughput to scale horizontally. We will examine the concrete mechanism Redis uses: 16,384 hash slots and a deterministic mapping function, and how nodes claim ranges of those slots. You will also learn how cluster-aware clients route commands to the right node, what happens when a client targets the wrong node and receives a MOVED redirection, and how hash tags let you group related keys into the same slot for multi-key commands. Finally, we will compare Redis Cluster’s combined sharding-plus-replication model to a master‑replica setup managed by Sentinel so you can decide which approach fits your application. By the end of this lesson you will be able to explain hash slots, compute slot placement for example keys, and recognize when hash tags are needed to keep multi-key operations working.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Redis Cluster shards data with 16,384 hash slots. Each key maps deterministically to a slot via CRC16 and nodes own ranges of slots so the dataset and throughput scale horizontally.

narration.text: These learning objectives break the chapter into practical skills you can use right away. First, you will understand sharding — why a single Redis master reaches limits on R A M and C P U and how partitioning the keyspace across nodes removes those limits. Second, you will be able to explain Redis Cluster architecture, including the 16,384 hash slots and the roles nodes play as masters and replicas for failover. Third, you will learn how data is deterministically mapped with CRC16 modulo 16,384 so you can predict where a key lives and reason about data locality. Fourth, you will identify the practical trade-offs: how Cluster enables linear scaling and automatic failover but constrains multi-key commands unless keys share a slot. Each objective includes a short mnemonic and a verified competency milestone to mark when you're ready to move on.

narration.text: Replication with Sentinel gives you high availability: a replica can take over when a master fails. But it does not increase the memory or write capacity of that master. A single master is limited by the R A M it holds and the C P U it uses for writes. So if your dataset grows beyond the memory of one server or your write throughput exceeds what one C P U can handle, replication simply copies that bottleneck instead of removing it. Sharding addresses this by dividing the dataset into separate partitions so different servers hold different subsets of keys. That way both storage and write throughput scale as you add nodes. A common misconception is to expect replicas to spread reads and writes evenly; while replicas can serve reads in many setups, writes still hit the master and the master’s resources remain the limit. Another misconception is that Sentinel adds sharding — it does not. Sentinel manages failover for a single-master topology. In contrast, Redis Cluster pairs sharding and replication: each master owns some slots and may have replicas to handle failover for those slots. As a practical example, imagine a cache that grows from 50GB to 300GB. A single master cannot hold 300GB without larger memory or swapping; sharding lets you split that dataset across many machines to avoid swapping and maintain low latency. Think about your application's read-write pattern: if writes are heavy or data is large, sharding with Cluster is the scalable option. How will you know when replication is no longer enough?

keyIdea.title: Don't conflate HA with scale
keyIdea.text: Replication provides failover but does not remove the single-master capacity limits; sharding is required to increase storage and write throughput horizontally.

content.html:
Core Concept Why replication alone doesn't scale
Definition

Replication duplicates data for availability, but the master still handles writes and holds the full dataset. That single-master resource profile creates a scaling ceiling.

  • • Replication = copies for failover and read replicas.
  • • Scaling = increasing capacity by adding machines (sharding).
  • • Sentinel manages failover, not partitioning.
Concrete scenario
A cache grows from 50GB to 300GB. A single master will swap or require much larger hardware. Sharding splits those 300GB across nodes so no single server is overloaded.
Key Takeaway

Use replication for availability; use sharding for capacity and throughput.

Comparison cards
Master + Sentinel
High availability for a single master, automatic failover via Sentinel. Does not split dataset.
Redis Cluster
Shards dataset across multiple masters and uses replicas for failover, combining scale and availability.
Common mistake
Relying on replicas to increase write throughput. Replicas do not accept writes; the master is the bottleneck.
Pro tip
Measure memory and write saturation on the master. When either is saturated, consider Cluster sharding.

screens.title: Sharding: partitioning the keyspace
screens.subtitle: What sharding means and why it matters

narration.text: Sharding is the process of partitioning a large dataset into smaller, independent pieces called shards. In Redis Cluster each shard is represented by a master node that owns a subset of the cluster's hash slots. The practical benefit is straightforward: each shard stores only a portion of the total dataset and handles a portion of the write load, so adding shards increases both memory capacity and aggregate write throughput. When designing sharding you must think about data locality and operations. Some operations — especially multi-key commands — require all keys to be colocated in the same slot. If keys are widely scattered across shards, certain operations will fail or require application-level coordination. A common analogy is a large library: instead of forcing every book on one shelf, you split the collection into sections so patrons can be served in parallel at different counters. A misconception is that sharding removes the need for replicas; it does not. Each shard can and should have replicas for high availability. Another design point is that sharding changes how you debug and operate the dataset: global scans and single-node assumptions are no longer valid. Consider sharding early when your dataset or throughput needs can exceed a single machine, and plan key naming with locality in mind so common multi-key operations remain possible.

keyIdea.title: Sharding principle
keyIdea.text: Split the logical dataset into smaller independent shards so storage and writes can scale across machines; plan key locality for multi-key operations.

content.html:
Definition
Sharding: partitioning the keyspace
Split a dataset into shards so each server holds part of the data and the write load is distributed.
Why it matters
  • • Increases total memory capacity by using many machines.
  • • Distributes write throughput so no single CPU is the bottleneck.
  • • Requires thought about operation locality and design of multi-key commands.
Analogy
A library split into sections lets multiple visitors be served at once. Sharding splits keys into sections so nodes serve requests in parallel.
Design considerations
Plan key names for locality to enable multi-key operations when needed.
Avoid relying on global commands like KEYS and SELECT in Cluster mode.
Give each master replicas for availability — sharding plus replication is common.

screens.title: Hash slots: 16,384 partitions
screens.subtitle: The deterministic slot model that powers Redis Cluster

narration.text: A central idea in Redis Cluster is the division of the entire keyspace into 16,384 logical hash slots. That fixed number gives a simple way to reason about distribution: each key is mapped to exactly one slot, and each node owns a set of slots. Ownership might be a contiguous range, for example node A owning 0–5000, node B owning 5001–10000, and node C owning 10001–16383. The mapping is deterministic so any client or tool can compute the slot for a key independently. This predictability enables cluster-aware clients to route commands directly to the correct node without consulting a central coordinator on every request. It also simplifies rebalancing: moving slots between nodes moves ranges of keys rather than individual keys one by one. A misconception is to think slots are physical partitions — slots are logical labels that keys map to; the actual data resides on the nodes that claim those slots. Understanding slots helps you plan shard counts and rebalancing actions because you can reason about ranges and their sizes. When combined with replicas, each slot's data is mirrored for availability. Consider the slot map as a lightweight directory the cluster uses to decide who owns what and how clients should send commands.

keyIdea.title: Slot model
keyIdea.text: Redis splits the keyspace into 16,384 logical slots. Nodes own slot ranges and the mapping is deterministic so clients can route commands to owners.

content.html:
Architecture
Hash slots: 16,384 partitions
How it works
The keyspace is divided into 16,384 slots. Each key deterministically maps to a slot so clients and nodes agree on ownership without a central coordinator.
Slot ranges are assigned to nodes. Moving slots moves groups of keys.
Replicas mirror the slots owned by a master for failover.
Clients compute slots locally using the same hashing rule.
Visual example
Node A
Slots 0–5000
Node B
Slots 5001–10000
Node C
Slots 10001–16383
Misconception

Slots are logical labels, not separate physical databases. The actual data lives on nodes that own those slots.

screens.title: How keys map to slots: CRC16(key) % 16384
screens.subtitle: Deterministic calculation you can run with redis-cli

narration.text: Redis uses a simple and deterministic rule to place keys into slots: compute the CRC16 checksum of the key string and take that value modulo 16,384. This yields an integer in the range 0 to 16,383 which is the slot number. Because the computation is deterministic, any client or tool can independently compute a key's slot and route the command to the node that owns that slot. Practically, redis-cli offers a helper: CLUSTER KEYSLOT key will print the slot number for you. For example, running CLUSTER KEYSLOT mykey will show the slot integer for the key named mykey. This is useful when testing hash tags and multi-key behavior. A common misconception is to assume hash functions or slot counts change often; the slot count is fixed at 16,384 for Redis Cluster, which simplifies reasoning but means you must plan your rebalancing strategy rather than rely on a dynamic slot count. A brief example you can try locally is to run cluster keyslot against several keys to observe that similar key patterns often map to different slots unless you use a hash tag. Remember, the mapping rule is CRC16(key) % 16384 — knowing that math lets you predict and design key names to achieve desired locality.

keyIdea.title: Slot math
keyIdea.text: Slot = CRC16(key) % 16384. Use CLUSTER KEYSLOT in redis-cli to verify where a key will land and to test hash tags.

content.html:
Process Flow
How keys map to slots
Deterministic rule used by clients and nodes.
Formula
CRC16(key) % 16384
You can verify slots locally with redis-cli CLUSTER KEYSLOT. This makes the mapping easy to test when you design keys.
Concrete example
redis-cli CLUSTER KEYSLOT mykey
redis-cli CLUSTER KEYSLOT user:1:profile
redis-cli CLUSTER KEYSLOT product:2:price
Why deterministic mapping helps
  • • Clients compute the slot locally and send commands straight to the owner node.
  • • If a node is queried for a key it doesn’t own, it returns a MOVED response to redirect the client.
  • • Rebalancing moves whole slot ranges, making slot-based rebalancing simpler than per-key moves.
Common-mistake
Assuming keys with similar text map to the same slot. They often won't unless you use hash tags to force locality.

screens.title: Masters and replicas: roles inside a cluster
screens.subtitle: How nodes share responsibilities for slots and failover

narration.text: In Redis Cluster each node has a role: a master that owns one or more hash slots, or a replica that mirrors a master for those slots. Masters are authoritative for the data in their slots and handle writes for those keys. Replicas maintain a copy of the master's data and are available to promote to master if the primary fails. This pairing gives you both horizontal scale and high availability: a cluster scales by adding more masters, and each master can have one or more replicas to avoid data loss during failover. Operationally, this means when a master fails the cluster can elect a replica and reassign slot ownership so the data remains accessible. A misconception is to expect replicas to automatically serve writes; replicas are read-only copies and will not accept writes for the master's slots unless promoted. Another practical note is that clients must be cluster-aware: they need to know which node currently owns a slot so that they send writes to the active master rather than a replica. Planning replica placement matters for availability and latency: place replicas on different failure domains so a single hardware failure doesn't remove both master and its replicas. What questions do you have about pairing masters and replicas in your deployment?

keyIdea.title: High availability pattern
keyIdea.text: Masters own slots and handle writes; replicas mirror masters and can be promoted to maintain availability after a master fails.

content.html:
Node Roles
Masters and replicas
Master responsibilities
  • • Owns a set of hash slots and the keys mapped to them.
  • • Handles write commands for those keys.
  • • May be paired with replicas for redundancy.
Replica responsibilities
  • • Mirrors its master's slots and data.
  • • Can be promoted to master during failover.
  • • Should be placed in different failure domains from its master.
Operational cards
Add masters to increase capacity. Each new master can take ownership of additional slot ranges.
Add replicas per master for failover. Replicas don’t expand write capacity.
Misconception: replicas increase write throughput. They do not; writes still go to the master.
Key Takeaway

Shard by adding masters; protect each master with replicas for automatic failover.

screens.title: Cluster-aware clients and MOVED redirection
screens.subtitle: How clients learn and correct routing mistakes

narration.text: Clients connecting to a Redis Cluster are typically cluster-aware. That means the client library either maintains knowledge of the cluster topology or learns it as it receives responses. When a client sends a command to a node that does not own the slot for the given key, the node replies with a MOVED redirection that includes the address of the correct node. A cluster-aware client can then retry the command at that address. This behavior reduces round trips in steady-state because clients compute slots and send commands directly to the owner node. However, during topology changes or if the client lacks a recent topology map, MOVED responses are how the cluster guides clients to the current owners. A common mistake is to hardcode a single node and expect that node to forward commands to the owner; Redis Cluster relies on clients to perform the redirection rather than the node proxying the command. For practical testing, run redis-cli against a node and observe MOVED responses when you intentionally target a wrong node for a key. Understanding MOVED redirections helps you design resilient retry logic in clients and reduces wasted requests during reconfiguration or failover.

keyIdea.title: Client routing
keyIdea.text: Cluster-aware clients compute slots and follow MOVED responses to retry on the correct node, ensuring commands reach the owner of a key.

content.html:
Process Flow
Cluster-aware clients and MOVED
Client behavior
  • • Compute slot for the key and send command to the node owning that slot.
  • • If node replies MOVED, retry against the provided node address.
  • • Maintain a topology cache to avoid repeated MOVED responses.
Example: redis-cli
# If you send a command to the wrong node you may see:
MOVED 12182 10.0.0.5:6379
# The client uses the provided address and retries the command.
Operational notes
Do not rely on a single node to proxy requests to the owner. Use cluster-aware clients or implement retry logic that follows MOVED responses. When topology rapidly changes, expect more MOVED responses until clients refresh their topology cache.
Common-mistake
Hardcoding a seed node and expecting all requests to be routed by that node. Redis Cluster expects clients to route to owners, not proxy through one node.

screens.title: Failover in Redis Cluster
screens.subtitle: How replicas take over when masters fail

narration.text: Redis Cluster provides automatic failover by promoting replicas when a master becomes unreachable. Each master can have one or more replicas that keep an up-to-date copy of the master's slots. If a master fails, the cluster performs a consensus process and promotes an eligible replica to become the new master for the affected slots. This preserves slot ownership and keeps the data accessible without manual intervention. It is important to plan replica placement so that a single failure domain does not remove both master and its replicas. A misconception is thinking that failover is instantaneous and without risk; promotions take time and there is a brief window where some clients may receive errors while the cluster updates slot ownership. Also, if replication lag exists, there is a possibility of losing very recent writes. For operational safety, ensure replicas are healthy and replication lag is low, and be prepared for brief transient errors during failover. After promotion, clients using cluster-aware libraries follow updated routing and resume operations, often with minimal disruption. How you configure replicas affects both recovery speed and data safety.

keyIdea.title: Automatic failover
keyIdea.text: Replicas can be promoted to master after a failure, preserving slot ownership and availability, but plan replica placement and monitor replication lag.

content.html:
Process Flow
Failover in Redis Cluster
What happens on failure
  • • The cluster detects an unreachable master.
  • • Eligible replicas are considered and one is promoted to master.
  • • Slot ownership is updated so clients can send commands to the new master.
Risk: replication lag means recent writes may not be present on the promoted replica.
Operational checklist
  • • Place replicas in separate failure domains from their masters.
  • • Monitor replication lag and replica health continuously.
  • • Expect brief transient errors during leader election and slot updates.
Key Takeaway

Automatic failover preserves availability but plan for short disruption and potential loss of the very latest writes if lag exists.

screens.title: Hash tags: forcing keys into the same slot
screens.subtitle: Use {...} to enable multi-key operations on related data

narration.text: Redis Cluster enforces that multi-key operations succeed only when all keys are in the same hash slot. To support patterns like retrieving related items together, Redis Cluster provides hash tags: a substring wrapped in curly braces that is used as the sole input to the slot hash. For example, user:{100}:profile and user:{100}:cart both compute the slot only from the string inside the braces, so they land in the same slot. This makes multi-key commands such as MGET or DEL work as expected for related keys. You can test this behavior using redis-cli CLUSTER KEYSLOT to see that keys with the same tag return the same slot number. A common mistake is to overuse hash tags and accidentally create hotspots, where too many keys map to the same slot and overload a single node. Use tags deliberately for related data that must be accessed together and balance shard usage with application needs. A brief example you can try is comparing CLUSTER KEYSLOT product:1:name with CLUSTER KEYSLOT product:{1}:name and observing the difference. Hash tags are a practical tool to reconcile multi-key semantics with a sharded architecture, but they require intentional key design.

keyIdea.title: Hash tag pattern
keyIdea.text: Place a substring in curly braces to force multiple keys into the same slot, enabling safe multi-key operations for related data.

content.html:
Definition
Hash tags: forcing keys into the same slot
Use {...} in key names so the bracketed substring is the only input to the slot hash.
Examples to run
redis-cli CLUSTER KEYSLOT product:1:name
redis-cli CLUSTER KEYSLOT product:2:price

redis-cli CLUSTER KEYSLOT product:{1}:name
redis-cli CLUSTER KEYSLOT product:{1}:price
You will observe that untagged keys usually map to different slots, while tagged keys with the same content inside braces map to the same slot.
When to use tags
  • • When related keys must be accessed or updated together with multi-key commands.
  • • When you can accept the performance trade-off that those keys concentrate on one node.
  • • Avoid tags when they would create a hotspot that overloads a single server.
Pro tip: use tags sparingly and intentionally to enable only those multi-key operations that truly need co-location.

screens.title: Limitations: commands and multi-key constraints
screens.subtitle: What Redis Cluster does not support and why it matters

narration.text: Redis Cluster enables scale but imposes limitations you must plan for. The most important constraint is that multi-key operations succeed only when all the keys are in the same hash slot; otherwise the command fails. That means commonly used commands like MGET, MSET, or transactions that touch multiple arbitrary keys will only work if keys are colocated. To enable co-location you can use hash tags, but that requires deliberate key naming and may cause hotspots. Another set of limitations involves commands that require a global dataset view. For example, KEYS — which iterates all keys — is not suitable in Cluster mode because there isn't a single node with a complete dataset. SELECT, which switches logical databases, is also unsupported because Cluster only uses database 0. A misconception is that you can simply run global admin commands and expect cluster-wide results; you must instead use node-level scans or client-side aggregation if you need cluster-wide data. When designing your application, ask whether your data model needs cross-key transactions or global scans; if it does, Cluster may complicate those patterns or require rethinking how you encode and access your data. These trade-offs are why planning the data model is as important as choosing the deployment topology.

keyIdea.title: Design constraints
keyIdea.text: Cluster limits multi-key operations to keys in the same slot and does not support global commands like KEYS or database selection with SELECT; design keys accordingly.

content.html:
Comparison
Limitations to plan for
Multi-key operations
Operations like MGET, MSET, or multi-key DEL require all keys to be in the same slot to succeed. Hash tags are the mechanism to achieve that when needed.
Common mistake: expecting cluster to transparently run multi-key commands across nodes. It will not.
Unsupported global features
  • • KEYS is not practical for cluster mode since keys are distributed.
  • • SELECT is unsupported; Cluster uses only database 0.
  • • Use node-level scans and aggregate results client-side if you must inspect the whole dataset.
Key Takeaway

Design your data model to avoid wide multi-key dependencies or use hash tags for related keys that must be accessed together.

screens.title: Benefits and trade-offs versus Sentinel master-replica
screens.subtitle: When to choose Redis Cluster over a Sentinel-managed setup

narration.text: Redis Cluster provides horizontal scaling by sharding data and pairing each master with replicas for failover, whereas a master-replica setup managed by Sentinel focuses on high availability for a single master. The main benefit of Cluster is the ability to store much larger datasets and handle more write throughput because you add masters to grow capacity. Cluster also offers automatic failover via replicas. The trade-offs include complexity in data modelling, limitations on multi-key operations unless keys share a slot, and the need for cluster-aware clients to route commands. Sentinel setups are simpler for applications that fit on a single machine and rely on replicas mostly for read scaling and failover; they avoid the multi-key constraints but do not expand the master’s memory or write capacity. A misconception is that Cluster always delivers better availability; availability depends on replica counts and placement in both models. Choose Cluster when your dataset or write load exceeds a single server and you can design keys for locality. Choose Sentinel when you need simplicity and the dataset comfortably fits on one master. Practical decisions hinge on your application's multi-key patterns, expected dataset size, and operational tolerance for complexity.

keyIdea.title: Choosing topology
keyIdea.text: Use Redis Cluster for horizontal scale and sharding; use Sentinel-managed master-replica if your dataset fits a single master and you prefer simpler operations.

content.html:
Comparison
Cluster vs. Sentinel
Redis Cluster
  • • Shards data across multiple masters for scale.
  • • Uses replicas for failover per shard.
  • • Requires cluster-aware clients and planning for multi-key constraints.
Master + Sentinel
  • • Simpler single-master topology with replicas for availability.
  • • Easier multi-key operations because the dataset is not partitioned.
  • • Does not increase master’s memory or write capacity.
Decision guidance
If your dataset or write load will exceed a single server, plan for Cluster. If your dataset fits comfortably on one master and you want simpler operations, use Sentinel. Evaluate multi-key requirements: if your app needs many cross-key transactions, consider whether key design or another scaling approach is required.

screens.title: Try it: slot mapping and hash tag experiments
screens.subtitle: Practical redis-cli commands to explore slot behavior

narration.text: This hands-on activity shows how to verify slot mappings and experiment with hash tags using redis-cli. Even without a running cluster, redis-cli can compute the slot for any key with CLUSTER KEYSLOT key. Try a few keys and observe the slot integers returned to see how keys are distributed. Next, try keys with and without hash tags to see how tags force co-location. For instance run CLUSTER KEYSLOT product:1:name and CLUSTER KEYSLOT product:2:price to see they usually land in different slots. Then run CLUSTER KEYSLOT product:{1}:name and CLUSTER KEYSLOT product:{1}:price and observe they share a slot. Reflect on whether an MGET across untagged keys would work: it would not if they map to different slots. This experiment gives you direct evidence of how slots and tags behave and helps you design key patterns that either distribute load evenly or keep related data together. After conducting these commands, consider how your application would handle multi-key operations and whether hash tags or a different partitioning strategy better suits your workload. screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders from this chapter

narration.text: Here are three compact ideas to carry forward. First: sharding partitions the data into shards so storage and write capacity can grow horizontally across multiple masters. Second: Redis Cluster uses 16,384 hash slots and a deterministic CRC16 modulus mapping so clients and nodes can agree on slot ownership. Third: cluster-aware clients route commands to owners and follow MOVED redirections when topology changes. Remember these core concepts as you design your keys and choose a topology. content.html:
Key Concepts
Sharding
Partition data into shards so capacity and throughput scale across nodes.
Hash Slots
16,384 logical slots; keys map with CRC16(key) % 16384.
Client Routing
Clients compute slots and follow MOVED redirections to the node that owns a slot.
Summary takeaway

Design keys with slot locality in mind and rely on cluster-aware clients to maintain efficient routing and availability.

narration.text: Keep these operational reminders close when you deploy Redis Cluster. First, multi-key operations require keys to be in the same slot; use hash tags to force co-location when the application needs it. Second, Cluster does not support commands that require a global dataset view such as KEYS or selecting multiple databases with SELECT; design alternatives or node-level scans with client aggregation. Third, plan replica placement across failure domains and monitor replication lag because promotions protect availability but do not guarantee zero data loss if lag exists. These reminders help you balance scale and operational safety in real deployments. Key Concepts
Hash Tags
Use braces to place related keys in the same slot for multi-key commands.
Unsupported commands
Avoid KEYS and SELECT in Cluster; use node scans or architecture changes instead.
Replica placement
Place replicas across failure domains and monitor lag to reduce failover risk.
Final takeaway

Plan your keys and topology together: locality, availability, and cluster limitations are interdependent decisions for a reliable, scalable Redis deployment.
